title: Classical Bits vs. Quantum Bits
summary: Start with the difference between a definite classical bit and a qubit described by amplitudes, then measure the simplest possible circuit.
objectives: Describe a classical bit as a definite 0 or 1.
Write a one-qubit state as a normalized combination of |0⟩ and |1⟩.
Explain why measurement returns one classical outcome even when the state has two amplitudes.

sections.heading: A classical bit is a definite choice
body: A classical bit stores exactly one value: 0 or 1. Reading it does not change it. A register of n classical bits stores one of 2^n definite strings, such as 0101.
Classical randomness can also produce 0 or 1, but the uncertainty is in our knowledge or in a random process, not in a stored superposition of two values.

sections.heading: A qubit carries amplitudes
body: A qubit is described by a state vector with two complex amplitudes. The amplitudes are not probabilities: they can be negative or complex, and they can interfere.
The squared magnitudes give the probabilities of the two computational-basis outcomes. Normalization says those probabilities add to one.

sections.heading: Measurement turns amplitudes into one bit
body: A computational-basis measurement returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|². After the measurement, the qubit is in the state corresponding to the observed outcome.
One shot therefore produces one classical bit. To see a distribution, we prepare and measure the circuit many times. Each preparation-and-measurement is called a shot.

callout.title: Precision matters
callout.text: A qubit with equal-magnitude amplitudes is not 'both 0 and 1' in the sense of storing two classical values you can read out. Measurement gives a single outcome; the amplitudes determine the statistics of many repetitions.

sections.heading: Try the simplest circuit
body: The example circuit prepares q0 in |0⟩ and immediately measures it. In an ideal simulator every shot should return 0.
After running it, return to the builder and insert an X gate before the measurement. X flips |0⟩ to |1⟩, so every shot should then return 1.

expected_behavior: Measurement of |0⟩ produces the bitstring "0" for all 1,024 shots in the ideal simulator.
Adding X before the measurement flips the definite outcome to "1" for all shots.
The counts are deterministic here; no 50/50 split should appear.

check_questions.question: A qubit is in the state (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2. What does a single computational-basis measurement return?
options: Either 0 or 1, with one observed value per shot
Always 0 because the amplitudes are positive
Nothing until a second qubit is measured
check_questions.explanation: Measurement yields one classical outcome. Over many shots the two outcomes appear with probabilities |1/√2|² = 1/2 each, but a single shot is one bit.

check_questions.question: What does the normalization condition |α|² + |β|² = 1 guarantee?
options: The amplitudes are always real numbers
The measurement probabilities sum to one
The qubit is entangled with another qubit
check_questions.explanation: The squared magnitudes are the probabilities of outcomes 0 and 1, so their sum must be 1.
